title: Modals
description: Master modal verbs for Grade 8: ability, permission, possibility, obligation and advice, plus modal perfects — with bilingual notes, examples, practice exercises and tests.

topics.title: Ability, Permission, Possibility & Obligation
topics.concept:
Each modal covers a few related meanings:

MeaningModalsExample
Abilitycan, could (past)I can / could swim.
Permissioncan (informal), may (formal), could (polite)May I leave?
Possibilitymay, might, couldIt might snow.
Obligationmust, have to, should, ought toYou must wear a seatbelt.
Certainty (deduction)must (positive), can't (negative)He must be tired; it can't be true.

must vs have to: 'must' is an inner/strong obligation; 'have to' is an external rule. mustn't vs needn't: 'mustn't' = it is forbidden; 'needn't' = it is not necessary.

examples.problem: Choose: You ___ (must / can) stop at a red light.
examples.solution: must — it is a strong obligation / rule.

examples.problem: Deduction: The lights are off; they ___ be out.

topics.title: Other Modals & Modal Perfects
topics.concept:
A few more useful forms:

  • need / needn't — necessity: You needn't worry.
  • used to — a past habit no longer true: She used to live here.
  • would — past habit or polite request: We would play here as kids; Would you help?
  • shall — offers/suggestions: Shall I open the window?

Modal perfects = modal + have + V3. They talk about the past:

  • must have done — certainty about the past: She's wet; it must have rained.
  • should have done — criticism/regret: You should have called.
  • could have done — an unrealised possibility: I could have won.
  • might have done — a past possibility: He might have missed the bus.

examples.problem: Modal perfect: The ground is wet. It ___ (rain) last night.
examples.solution: must have rained — a confident deduction about the past.

examples.problem: Choose: You ___ (should have / must have) told me earlier. (criticism)
examples.solution: should have told me — it expresses criticism about something not done.

recap: Modal perfect = modal + have + V3 (talks about the past)
must have = past certainty; should have = regret; could/might have = past possibility

questions.q: '___ I use your phone?' (polite)
'He ___ run very fast as a boy.'
'You ___ wear a seatbelt.' (rule)
'You ___ see a dentist.' (advice)
Correct form:
'It's cloudy; it ___ rain.' (possibility)
'You ___ worry; it's all done.' (not necessary)
'He's not answering; he ___ be asleep.' (deduction)
'I ___ live in Pune, but now I live in Delhi.'
questions.explanation: Past habit no longer true → 'used to'.

questions.q: 'You ___ have called me!' (regret)
'___ I carry that for you?' (offer)
Meaning of 'You can't be serious!'
options: It seems impossible/I don't believe it.

questions.q: Choose the correct modal perfect: 'The cake is gone; the children ___ it.'
Spot the error: 'He must has finished by now.'
questions.explanation: Modal perfect uses 'have', not 'has': 'must have finished'.

questions.q: Which sentence shows criticism of a past action?
questions.explanation: 'should have + V3' criticises an undone past action.

questions.q: Choose the correct meaning: 'You needn't have bought milk.'
options: It was forbidden to buy milk.
Buying milk was unnecessary (but you did).
questions.explanation: 'needn't have + V3' = an action that was done but was unnecessary.

questions.q: Fill in: 'She ___ the answer; she's a brilliant student.' (near-certain present)
Choose: 'Passengers ___ fasten their seatbelts during take-off.' (rule)
Rearrange: 'have / you / me / could / warned'
questions.explanation: 'You could have warned me.' (an unrealised past possibility).

questions.q: Which is correct for a polite request?
options: Would you mind to help me?
questions.explanation: 'Would you mind + gerund' is the polite request form.

outcomes: Use modal verbs to show ability, permission, possibility and obligation
Choose the right modal for advice, necessity and deduction
Use 'have to', 'ought to', 'need' and 'used to' correctly
Form and understand modal perfects (must have done, etc.)

intro.en: Modal verbs — can, could, may, might, will, would, shall, should, must, ought to — are helping verbs that add meaning: they show how possible, necessary, or advisable something is. They never change form (no -s, no -ing) and are always followed by the base verb: She can swim, not 'She cans swim'.
intro.hi: सहायक क्रियाएँ / Modals — can, could, may, might, will, would, shall, should, must, ought to — ऐसी helping verbs हैं जो अर्थ जोड़ती हैं: ये बताती हैं कि कोई बात कितनी संभव, आवश्यक या उचित है। ये कभी रूप नहीं बदलतीं (न -s, न -ing) और हमेशा मूल क्रिया के साथ आती हैं: She can swim, न कि 'She cans swim'।

real_life.situation:
A few quick exchanges in a day:

Class: May I come in? — You may.
Road: You must wear a helmet.
Friend: You should see a doctor.
real_life.why: Each modal carries a precise shade of meaning: may asks formal permission, must states a strong rule, should gives advice. Picking the right modal is the difference between sounding polite, firm, or merely suggestive.

rule_box.html:
ModalMain useExample
can / couldability, permissionShe can swim.
may / mightpermission, possibilityIt may rain.
must / have tonecessity, obligationYou must stop.
should / ought toadvice, dutyYou should rest.
shall / will / wouldfuture, offer, requestShall I help?
rule_box.formula: Modal + base verb (no 'to', except 'ought to' / 'have to')
rule_box.example: He must go now; she ought to apologise; we can wait.

common_mistakes.note: After most modals, use the base verb without 'to'.

items.q: You ______ wear a helmet on a bike. (obligation)

fill_l2.instructions: Complete with a modal or modal perfect.

items.q: The streets are wet; it ______ (rain) last night.
She ______ (live) here as a child, but she moved away.

error_detection.sentence: You should have come yesterday but you didn't, you should came.
It is raining, you mustn't take an umbrella if you don't want to.
error_detection.correct: It is raining, you needn't take an umbrella if you don't want to.

sentence_correction.wrong: You must to wear a uniform.
He must has missed the train.
sentence_correction.correct: He must have missed the train.

reading.passage: "You must submit the project by Friday," the teacher said. "You should start today, and you may ask me for help. You needn't print it in colour — black and white is fine. If your file is missing, you must have deleted it by mistake; you should have made a backup. You could have used the cloud."

questions.q: Which modal shows a strong obligation, and which gives advice?
questions.answer: 'must' (must submit) shows obligation; 'should' (should start) gives advice.

questions.q: Explain the meaning of 'You needn't print it in colour.'
questions.answer: It is not necessary to print in colour — 'needn't' = no obligation.

questions.q: What does 'you must have deleted it' express?
questions.answer: A confident deduction about the past (near-certainty) using the modal perfect.

speaking: You must finish your homework first.
She can play the piano beautifully.

writing.prompt: Write five sentences of advice and rules for a new student, using must, should, can, may and needn't.
writing.example: You must reach by 8. You should keep your ID. You can use the library. You may ask any teacher. You needn't bring lunch on Fridays.

micro_quiz.q: 'She ___ swim when she was five.' (past ability)

challenge.q: Choose the correct meaning: 'You mustn't park here.'
options: It is not necessary to park here.
It is forbidden to park here.

challenge.q: Which modal perfect fits? 'I'm not sure, but he ___ missed the bus.'
challenge.explanation: 'might have' shows an uncertain past possibility.
